sections.content: You know *me alegra que* with the subjunctive from A2 Unit 27 and the present perfect subjunctive from B1 Unit 37. In lively everyday speech, speakers compress emotional reactions into exclamations: *¡Qué raro que…!*, *¡Qué pena que…!*, *¡Qué suerte que…!*, *¡Qué lástima que…!*. Because they react to a fact rather than report it neutrally, they take the subjunctive — very often the **present perfect subjunctive** for something that just happened (*¡Qué raro que no haya llamado todavía!*, *¡Qué pena que se haya quemado el bizcocho!*). Watch one famous exception: *menos mal que* ('thank goodness') always takes the **indicative** (*¡Menos mal que trajiste el guiso!*).

sections.title: Conversational exclamations: subjunctive vs indicative
rows: *¡Qué raro que no haya llegado todavía!* (reaction to a recent fact).
*¡Qué pena que se haya quemado el bizcocho!* (regret).
*¡Qué suerte que hayan venido todos a merendar!* (relief/joy).
*¡Menos mal que guardamos un poco de guiso!* (exception: ALWAYS indicative).

items.spanish: ¡Qué raro que no haya llamado todavía si suele llegar puntual!
items.english: How strange that she hasn't called yet when she usually arrives on time!

items.spanish: ¡Qué pena que se haya quemado el bizcocho justo antes de merendar!
items.english: What a shame that the sponge cake burned right before afternoon tea!

items.spanish: ¡Qué suerte que no te hayas atragantado al comer tan rápido!
items.english: How lucky that you didn't choke while eating so fast!

items.spanish: ¡Menos mal que preparaste un picoteo para calmar el antojo!
items.english: Thank goodness you prepared some snacks to satisfy the craving!

sections.content: Two points to keep sharp in fast conversation: use *haya / hayas / hayan* + participle after *¡Qué raro que…!* when reacting to a recent completed event, and never put the subjunctive after *¡Menos mal que…!* (*Menos mal que viniste*, never *Menos mal que vinieras*).
